original_question: Let M_n be the n-th term of the mirror sequence formed by writing the descending string from n to 1 immediately followed by the ascending string from 2 back to n, so the sequence begins 1, 212, 32123, 4321234, 543212345, and continues in the same way. Are there infinitely many prime numbers among these mirror-sequence terms, or only finitely many?
target_in_paper: The draft is targeting the paper's item 5) "Mirror Sequence" on page 5, where Smarandache lists the sequence 1, 212, 32123, 4321234, 543212345, 65432123456, 7654321234567, 876543212345678, 98765432123456789, 109876543212345678910, 1110987654321234567891011, ... and asks: "Question: How many of them are primes?" ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft identifies the correct sequence, gives the correct initial terms, and focuses on the primality of its terms, which is exactly the issue raised in item 5 of the paper. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
missing_details: The paper's official name for this sequence is "Mirror Sequence," and it appears as item 5 in the opening list of problems. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
The indexing should be explicit: the terms are indexed by positive integers n >= 1, beginning with M_1 = 1. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

The construction should be stated as decimal concatenation of whole integers n, n-1, ..., 1, 2, ..., n, not merely of single digits; this matters from n = 10 onward, as the paper explicitly lists 109876543212345678910. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

The paper does not state an arbitrary-base version for item 5, so the faithful stand-alone question should stay in ordinary base 10 rather than adding a base-B generalization. By contrast, such a generalization is explicitly mentioned for items 1 and 3. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

The paper's wording asks for the exact prime content of the sequence ("How many of them are primes?") rather than only the weaker finite-versus-infinite dichotomy. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
Because item 5 gives examples but no formal nth-term formula, a stand-alone rewrite should supply an explicit definition of M_n. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
refined_question: In base 10, for each integer n >= 1, let M_n be the integer obtained by concatenating the decimal expansions of n, n-1, ..., 2, 1, 2, ..., n-1, n; thus M_1 = 1, M_2 = 212, M_3 = 32123, and M_10 = 109876543212345678910. How many terms of this Mirror Sequence are prime numbers? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
justification: The match is exact: the user's sample terms coincide verbatim with item 5) "Mirror Sequence" in the paper, and the paper's own open question there is "How many of them are primes?" This is distinct from the nearby item 3) "Symmetric Sequence," whose terms begin 1, 11, 121, 1221, ... and therefore is not the target. To make the question stand alone while staying faithful to the paper, the only necessary sharpening is to state the decimal-concatenation rule explicitly; the paper itself supplies examples rather than a separate formal nth-term definition. Also, unlike items 1 and 3, item 5 is not presented with an arbitrary-base generalization, so the refined question should remain narrowly about the decimal Mirror Sequence. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
